newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Tough line on Russian oil debtors welcome - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Tough line on Russian oil debtors welcome - analysts.

text.p: Russia's hardening stance on energy sector debtors will come as a slap in the face for cash-strapped oil companies, but painful measures are the only way out of the non-payments crisis, oil analysts said Wednesday.
"These moves are excellent. They will penalise non-payers, and they are the only way to enforce payment," Ivan Mazalov, oil and gas analyst at CentreInvest Securities in Moscow, said.

Measures put forward this week to address the burning tax debt question ranged from bond issues for the YUKOS group to share issues for Sibneft, culminating on Tuesday in a bankruptcy threat against the main production unit of Tyumen Oil.
"These are steps in the right direction and could lead to payments of at least some of the accumulated tax arrears," said Alexei Kokin, oil and gas analyst at Renaissance Capital.
But Kokin said he was concerned share issues may not be the ideal solution to solving arrears problems, because they could infringe on shareholders' rights through share value dilution.

Analysts also said the key to a longer-term solution of tax arrears in Russia, including those of the energy sector, was a new Tax Code. The government hopes to have the new code in force from the beginning of next year.
This week's clampdown could also affects Russia's huge monopoly electricity group Unified Energy System (UES) and gas monopoly Gazprom.
First Deputy Fuel and Energy Minister Sergei Kiriyenko said on Tuesday the government is considering transferring assets from UES to Gazprom as a way of paying off inter-company debts.

The harshest measure so far was First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais' decision to start bankruptcy proceedings against Nizhnevartovskneftegaz after refusing to allow the company to restructure its tax debts.

The firm is the main production unit of Tyumenskaya Neftyanaya Kompaniya (Tyumen Oil), one of Russia's biggest oil group by output. It owed the government 1.17 trillion roubles ($200 million) in taxes as of May 1.

On the same day, the government meted out far less stringent conditions for fellow debtor Noyabrskneftegaz NYGS.RTS, the main production unit of OAO Sibirskaya Neftyanaya Kompaniya (Sibneft). Sibneft is similar in size to Tyumen Oil.
Noyabrskneftegaz owed a total 1.47 trillion roubles ($255 million) in taxes as of May 1, and Moscow accepted its plan to raise capital by issuing shares to pay off debts.
Analysts said Nizhnevartovskneftegaz probably would not be made bankrupt despite Tuesday's decision, and that production was unlikely to be affected by its cash crunch.
"I don't think the state will actually carry out the bankruptcy, because the company is one of the biggest in Russia and actually supports the city of Nizhnevartovsk," said one.
Nizhnevartovskneftegaz may have got the harshest of the two verdicts because of its weaker financial position, he added.

"Nizhnevartovskneftegaz is a tired, battered old giant, and among the worst of Russia's oil majors, because operating costs are among the highest," he said. "It will find it harder to pay off debts (than Noyabrskneftegaz)."
One senior tax official on Wednesday held out the prospect of a tax amnesty next year, when the new tax code is in force, for debtors which genuinely cannot pay.

But political motives behind the two decisions were not ruled out. Analysts said the government may have made the bankruptcy announcement to decrease competition in a planned investment tender for 40 percent of Tyumen Oil.
The Central Fuel Company, based in the political heartland of Moscow, would be one beneficiary, if it bids for the Tyumen stake as several analysts expect.
Shock therapy may be the only way to cure the energy sector's debt disease, which is often caused by inefficiency and even corruption, analysts said.

"All Russian (oil) firms say they have big problems with extracting oil. But you have to take this with a pinch of salt. It is often a convenient way to cover up stealth," one said. "This will go on forever unless strict measures are taken."
And only a team with the politicial clout of Chubais, and dynamic young reformer and First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, has a chance of success.
"Chubais and Nemtsov are working on measures, and I'm optimistic (they will succeed)," Mazalov said.
